head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Sum of the window `nums[i..i+k-1]`, built with a sliding window: add the new element, drop the old one
Fixed-size window sums in O(1) each
Index of the best window starting at or before `i` (first one on ties)
Index of the best window starting at or after `i`; `>=` makes ties favour the EARLIER start
The middle window must leave `k` positions on each side so the three don't overlap
Best window entirely to the left / right of the middle
Strictly greater keeps the lexicographically smallest tuple on ties
The problem asks for the lexicographically smallest indices

p: `nums = [1, 2, 1, 2, 6, 7, 5, 1]`, `k = 2`. Window sums `w = [3, 3, 3, 8, 13, 12, 6]`; best-left `[0, 0, 0, 3, 4, 4, 4]`; best-right `[4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6]`. Trying each possible middle window:
With the middle fixed, the left and right windows are independent choices from disjoint ranges, so each is just a precomputed best. Trying all middles is O(n). Brute force over all triples is O(n³).

blocks.h: Why do ties differ in the two passes?
p: `left` uses `>` so it keeps the earliest best window; `right` uses `>=` while scanning from the right so it also ends up with the earliest. Both then give the lexicographically smallest indices among equal sums.

689.takeaway: Three non-overlapping windows: precompute window sums, best-left and best-right, then try every middle window.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Sorts the dict's KEYS (the distinct words) with a key function
Custom ordering without writing a comparator
Tuple key: frequency descending (negated), then alphabetical ascending
Multi-criteria sort: the tuple breaks ties left to right
The first `k` of the sorted list

p: `["i","love","leetcode","i","love","coding"]`, `k = 2`:

`sorted` is ascending. Negating turns 'larger count first' into 'smaller key first'. The second element, the word itself, sorts alphabetically in the normal ascending direction, which is exactly the tie-break the problem wants.

A heap of size k gives O(n log k): `heapq.nsmallest(k, cnt, key=…)` with the same key. The full sort is O(n log n) and is simpler; mention the heap when the interviewer asks to do better than sorting.

bullets: Time: O(n + m log m) for m distinct words.

692.takeaway: Top-k frequent words: sort the distinct words with the key `(-count, word)` and slice.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Returns the size of the island containing (r, c), and sinks it as it goes
Largest island; `default=0` for an empty grid, and a generator avoids building a list

p: `[[0,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,1]]`: the scan starts a DFS at each cell, but only land cells return a positive size.

blocks.h: Why does sinking make the generator safe?
p: After the island at (0,1) is sunk, the later cells (1,0) and (1,1) return 0 immediately, so each island is counted once, from its first cell in scan order. Without sinking, one island would be measured many times and counted repeatedly.

695.takeaway: Max area of island: DFS flood fill that sinks cells and returns the component size; take the maximum.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Each subset must sum to exactly `total / k`
Place the big numbers first: they have the fewest placements, so dead ends appear early
A number bigger than the target can't go anywhere
Current sum of each of the `k` subsets being filled
Assign each number to a bucket
Skip buckets with the same current sum: they are interchangeable, so trying one is enough
Undo the placement when the recursion fails

p: `[4,3,2,3,5,2,1]`, `k = 4`: total 20, target 5, sorted `[5, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1]`. The first steps of the search (assign, then undo on failure):
Two empty buckets (both sum 0) lead to identical futures, so trying the second is wasted work. Skipping buckets with an already-tried sum cuts the search by a factor of up to k! on symmetric states.

head: Version
Search
rows: tries every bucket for every number: up to k^n
tries one bucket per distinct sum

p: Large numbers constrain the buckets most. Placing them first fills buckets quickly and detects impossible cases near the top of the recursion tree instead of deep in it.

bullets: Time: O(k^n) worst case, far less with pruning (the problem is NP-hard); a bitmask DP over subsets gives O(n · 2^n).

698.takeaway: Partition into k equal subsets: backtrack placing big numbers first into buckets, skipping buckets with equal sums and any overflow.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The new leaf, created up front
Inserting into an empty tree makes the new node the root
Walk down from the root like a BST search
BST ordering decides the direction (equal values go right; the problem guarantees no duplicates)
Stop at the first empty child slot and attach there
New values are always inserted as leaves

blocks.h: Why can the new node always be a leaf?
p: Searching for `val` ends at an empty child, and an empty child position is exactly where `val` would be found if it existed. Attaching there keeps every ancestor's ordering valid, and no existing node needs restructuring (unlike an AVL or red-black tree, which rebalances).

bullets: Time: O(h): O(log n) balanced, O(n) for a skewed tree.

701.takeaway: BST insert: search for the value, and attach a new leaf at the first empty child slot you hit.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Closed range `[lo, hi]` of candidate indices
Exact-match search; both ends are still possible answers
Continue while the range is non-empty
With a closed range, `lo == hi` is a valid one-element range
Guarantees the range shrinks every iteration

p: With a closed range and exact matching, each step tests `mid` and discards it. The loop must run when `lo == hi` (one candidate left), hence `<=`. Mixing styles (for example `hi = mid` with `lo <= hi`) can loop forever on a one-element range.

704.takeaway: Plain binary search: closed range, `lo <= hi`, and move past `mid` on every miss.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: A dummy head: the real first node is `head.next`
Removes the 'insert/delete at index 0' special case
Index validation without walking the list
`prev = head; for _ in range(index): prev = prev.next`
Walk to the node BEFORE the target position
Inserting or deleting needs the predecessor
Insert: the new node points at the old successor, then `prev` points to it, in one line

p: `addAtHead(1)`, `addAtTail(3)`, `addAtIndex(1, 2)`, `get(1)`:

blocks.h: Why a dummy head and a size field?
p: The dummy makes index 0 behave like any other position: the predecessor always exists. The size makes bounds checks O(1) (`index > size` rejects an insert past the tail, and `index >= size` rejects a get/delete of a non-existing node).
`addAtTail` walks the whole list: O(n). Keeping a `tail` pointer makes it O(1) but adds bookkeeping when deleting the last node; a doubly linked list speeds up deletion by index from the back.

bullets: Time: O(index) for get, add and delete at an index; O(n) for addAtTail here.

707.takeaway: Singly linked list design: dummy head for uniform edge cases, a size counter for validation, and a walk to the predecessor for every edit.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The number of allowed values: pick uniformly from `[0, k)`
Shrink the sampling range to exactly the count of valid values
A generator of allowed numbers in `[k, n)` (those not blacklisted)
Spare slots to receive remapped values
Each blacklisted number below `k` → an allowed number from the upper part
Remap bad picks to good ones
If `r` is blacklisted return its replacement, otherwise `r` itself

p: `n = 7`, blacklist `[2,3,5]`: allowed values are 0, 1, 4, 6, so `k = 4`. Blacklisted numbers below 4 are 2 and 3; allowed numbers in `[4, 7)` are 4 and 6, giving the map {2: 4, 3: 6}.

The four draws 0, 1, 2, 3 map to the four distinct allowed values 0, 1, 4, 6, one each. The mapping is a bijection between `[0, k)` and the allowed set, so each valid number has probability exactly 1/k.

blocks.h: Why only blacklisted numbers below k are mapped?
p: Draws are in `[0, k)`. Numbers at or above `k` are never drawn, so they need no entry. The count of free numbers in `[k, n)` equals the count of blacklisted numbers in `[0, k)`, so the `next(free)` calls never run out.

bullets: Time: O(n - k + b) ≈ O(b) to build; O(1) per pick.

710.takeaway: Random pick with a blacklist: sample from `[0, n - |blacklist|)` and remap any blacklisted draw to an allowed number from the top range.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Every product of positive integers is ≥ 1, so nothing can be `< k`; also prevents an endless shrink loop
Sliding window with a multiplicative condition
Shrink from the left until the product is valid again; division is exact because `nums[left]` is a factor of `prod`
Maintaining a window by removing the oldest element
Number of valid subarrays ENDING at `right`: one for each start from `left` to `right`
Growing the window can only increase the product
Required for the window to be monotone

p: If the window `[left, right]` has product `< k`, every sub-window that ends at `right` and starts at or after `left` also has product `< k` (fewer positive factors). That is exactly `right - left + 1` of them, and no subarray ending at `right` is counted twice.

bullets: Time: O(n), each pointer moves at most n times.

713.takeaway: Count subarrays with product < k: sliding window over positives; each right end contributes `right − left + 1` subarrays.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Each entry stores its value and the maximum of everything below and including it
Dig down to the TOP-MOST maximum, setting aside everything above it
The max is somewhere in the middle of the stack
Put the set-aside items back in their original order, recomputing their stored maxima

p: Pushing `5, 1, 5` then `popMax()` removes the TOP-most 5 (the problem requires the top-most when there are ties). Entries are `(value, max so far)`:
Pushing `5, 1, 2` and calling `popMax()` pops `2` and `1` into `buf`, removes the `5`, then pushes `1` and `2` back:

blocks.h: Why must the stored maxima be recomputed on re-push?
p: The pairs below the removed maximum were correct, but the re-pushed items carried a maximum that included the deleted value. Pushing them again recomputes `max(x, previous max)`, so the invariant holds.

blocks.h: When to choose a different design
p: If `popMax` is frequent, use a doubly linked list plus a sorted structure (a heap with lazy deletion or a balanced tree) to get O(log n) for all operations; this version optimises the common O(1) operations.

bullets: Time: O(1) for push/pop/top/peekMax; O(n) for popMax.

716.takeaway: Max stack: store (value, running max) per entry; popMax digs down to the top-most max, removes it, and replays the rest.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Sorted, so the distance between two items is the difference of their positions' values
Search over the ANSWER (a distance), from 0 to the largest possible
Number of pairs with distance `≤ mid`
Monotone count: it never decreases as `mid` grows
For each `i`, `j` is the leftmost index with `nums[i] - nums[j] ≤ mid`, so `i - j` pairs end at `i`
Two pointers that only move forward (sorted data)
At least k pairs are within `mid`: the answer is `≤ mid`, keep `mid`

p: `nums = [1,3,1]` sorts to `[1,1,3]`, `k = 1`. Pair distances are 0, 2, 2. The smallest is 0:

blocks.h: Why binary search the distance rather than the pairs?
p: There are n(n−1)/2 pairs; listing and sorting them costs O(n² log n). Counting pairs within a given distance takes O(n) with two pointers, and the count is monotone, so binary search over the distance range needs only log(max distance) rounds.

head: Approach
Time
rows: Min-heap of neighbouring pairs, pop k times
O(n log n + k log n)
O(n log n + n log D)

blocks.h: Why the `j` pointer never moves backward
p: If `nums[i] - nums[j] > mid`, then for the next `i` (larger value) the same `j` is also too far left, so `j` can only increase. That makes the count O(n) per probe instead of O(n²).

bullets: Time: O(n log n + n log(max − min)).

719.takeaway: k-th smallest pair distance: binary search on the distance, counting pairs within it with two pointers on the sorted array.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Are we inside a `/* … */` comment (can span lines)?
Characters kept so far for the current OUTPUT line; it survives across source lines while a block comment is open
Lines merge: text before `/*` joins text after `*/`
The next two characters, to detect `/*`, `*/`, `//`
Skip BOTH characters of the token so `/*/` isn't read as open and close
Ignore the rest of the line (but only outside a block)
Emit a line only when no block comment is open and there is content
Skip empty lines; keep merging while the block continues

p: `['a/*comment', 'line', 'more_comment*/b']`:

`a/*comment` + `...*/b` should become one output line `ab`. The text before the comment start and the text after its end belong to the same output line, so the buffer is only flushed when the block is closed.

blocks.h: Why does `//` not break inside a block?
p: The branch order checks `block` first. While a block comment is open, `//` is just ordinary comment text and is ignored.

bullets: Space: O(total characters) for the output.

722.takeaway: Remove comments with a small state machine: a `block` flag plus a buffer that carries over lines until the block comment closes.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: A third booking must not touch these
Overlap test for half-open intervals `[s, e)`; touching ends do not overlap
Reject if the new booking overlaps any double-booked region (that would be a triple booking)
The intersection of the new booking with an existing one becomes a double-booked region

blocks.h: Why check `over` first, and update afterwards?
p: If the first loop rejects the booking, no state may change. Adding intersections to `over` before knowing the booking is valid would leave phantom double-booked regions. Order: validate against `over`, then record new overlaps, then accept.

head: Approach
book
Space
rows: Sweep over a sorted map of +1/−1 events

p: `10-40` overlaps `10-20` once, so the intersection `(10,20)` becomes double-booked and the booking is accepted. `5-15` then overlaps the double-booked `(10,20)` and would make three bookings at 10 to 15, so it is rejected.

731.takeaway: Calendar II: keep bookings plus the double-booked intersections; reject any booking that overlaps a double-booked region.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Union-Find forest over WORDS (strings are the nodes)
Union-Find over arbitrary keys, not just 0..n-1
First time a word is seen, make it its own root
Union: merge the groups of the two similar words
Similarity is transitive, so groups are connected components
Equal words are similar even if they were never in a pair; otherwise they must share a root

p: Pairs `great~fine`, `drama~acting`, `skills~talent`:

blocks.h: Why Union-Find and not a direct pair set?
p: Problem 734 (Similarity I) is non-transitive, so a set of pairs is enough. Here similarity IS transitive: `a~b` and `b~c` means `a~c`. Union-Find groups transitively related words and answers 'same group?' in nearly O(1).

bullets: Time: O((P + n) · α) for P pairs and n words.

737.takeaway: Transitive similarity = connected components: Union-Find over words, then compare each position by root.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Total points available for value `v`: `v` times its count
Collapse duplicates: taking one `v` means deleting all neighbours but you can take every copy of `v`
Best total if we TAKE value `v`
Best total if we SKIP value `v`
Taking `v` is allowed only if we skipped `v - 1`
Skipping `v` leaves the best of the previous two states
Both new values use the OLD `take` and `skip`

p: `nums = [3,4,2]` gives points array `[0, 0, 2, 3, 4]` (value → total points):

Choosing value `v` forbids `v - 1` and `v + 1`, just like robbing a house forbids its neighbours. Once you bucket equal values into one cell of `pts`, the problem is exactly 'pick non-adjacent cells to maximise the sum' (problem 198).

The array has length `max(nums) + 1`, which is wasteful when values are huge but few. Sorting the distinct values and treating only consecutive ones as conflicting gives O(n log n) time independent of the value range.

740.takeaway: Delete and Earn reduces to House Robber over a points-per-value array: take = skip + pts[v], skip = max(take, skip).

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Adjacency list of directed weighted edges
Min-heap of `(distance, node)`, starting at the source
The unfinished node with the smallest tentative distance: its distance is now final (weights are non-negative)
Lazy deletion: stale heap entries for already-finalised nodes are skipped
The heap has no decrease-key, so duplicates are pushed and ignored
The signal reaches every node when the LAST node is finalised; unreachable nodes mean -1
Answer is the maximum shortest distance

blocks.h: Why is the answer the MAX of the shortest distances?
p: The signal travels along all paths in parallel, so each node receives it at its shortest-path time. Everyone has the signal only when the slowest node does, i.e. the maximum.

blocks.h: Why can we skip finalised nodes safely?
p: With non-negative weights, the first time a node is popped it has the smallest possible distance. Any later entry for it has a larger or equal distance and can't improve anything.

743.takeaway: Network delay = Dijkstra from the source; the answer is the largest finalised distance, or -1 if some node is unreachable.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Minimum cost to stand on step `i` (the top is step `len(cost)`)
DP where each state depends on the previous two
Minimum cost to stand on step `i - 1`
Come from step `i-1`: pay to leave it
Come from step `i-2`: pay to leave it
You may start on step 0 or 1 for free: standing there costs nothing, leaving costs

p: `cost = [1,100,1,1,1,100,1]`: after each step, `a` and `b` are the minimum costs to reach the previous step and the current step.

The top is one past the last step. The cost array is the cost of LEAVING each step, so reaching the top from step `n-1` or `n-2` costs `cost[n-1]` or `cost[n-2]`, which is what the final iteration `i = n` computes.

746.takeaway: Min cost climbing stairs: a two-variable DP where the cost to reach step i is the cheaper of arriving from i−1 or i−2.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: `1` = infected, `0` = healthy, `-1` = contained (walled off, permanently dead)
Encoding cell states in the grid itself
Collects one region: its `cells`, its `front` (set of distinct healthy cells it would infect next), and `perim` (the number of walls needed, counting each region-to-healthy edge)
A region is a connected component of infected cells
`front` is a set; `perim` is a counter
A healthy cell touched from two sides counts once in `front` but needs two walls, so the walls count edges, not cells
Contain the region that threatens the MOST distinct healthy cells
The problem's rule: wall the region with the largest threat
Mark it dead so later BFS rounds ignore it (only `== 1` counts as infected)
`g[a][b] = 1` for fronts of the other regions
Everything else spreads simultaneously, after the containment choice
If the most threatening region threatens nothing, the virus can't spread any more

p: A 4×8 grid: two regions, a vertical pair on the left (column 1) and a 3-cell column on the right (column 7). `#` = contained.

Total walls 5 + 5 = 10. In round 1 the left region threatens 5 cells, the right 4, so the left is walled; the right then spreads one step. In round 2 the grown right region is the only region and is walled.

blocks.h: Why count walls with `perim` and threats with `front`?
p: The cost to contain a region is the number of boundaries between infected and healthy cells, and a healthy cell with two infected neighbours needs two walls. The choice of region, however, depends on how many DISTINCT healthy cells are at risk. Using one number for both would pick the wrong region or the wrong cost.

bullets: Time: O((m·n)²) worst case: up to O(m·n) rounds, each a full BFS pass over O(m·n) cells.

749.takeaway: Contain Virus is a day-by-day simulation: BFS the regions, wall the one threatening the most healthy cells (counting edges as walls), let the rest spread.

If the start itself is dead, no move is possible
BFS queue and visited set of 4-digit strings
Shortest path in an unweighted state graph
Process one BFS level (= one wheel turn) at a time
Turn a wheel up or down, wrapping 9→0 and 0→9; Python's `%` keeps the result non-negative
Build the new state by replacing one character
`nxt not in seen and nxt not in dead`

p: Target `0202` with the dead ends `0201 0101 0102 1212 2002` is reached after 6 turns. Number of states in each BFS level (a state has 8 neighbours):

Every turn costs 1, so the fewest turns is the shortest path in an unweighted graph of 10,000 states. BFS reaches each state at its minimum depth, so the first time `target` is dequeued the depth is minimal.

Result

p: Bidirectional BFS from both `0000` and the target meets in the middle and explores far fewer states (about the square root of the work in a branching-heavy graph).

bullets: Time: O(10⁴ · 8 · 4) in the worst case: 10,000 states, each with 8 neighbours built from 4-character strings.

752.takeaway: Open the lock = BFS over 4-digit states with 8 neighbours each, skipping dead ends; the level at which the target appears is the answer.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Simulate one water drop at a time
Try LEFT first, then RIGHT: the problem's priority order
`i` walks outward; `best` is the lowest reachable spot found so far (starts at the drop position)
Water keeps flowing while the next cell is not higher (equal cells are walked across)
Update `best` only on a STRICT drop, so among equal-height spots the one nearest to `k` wins
Closest to the start among the lowest
If it found somewhere lower on the left, the drop settles there and the right side is not tried
`else` runs only if the loop did not `break`: neither side has a lower spot, so the drop stays at `k`

p: `heights = [2,1,1,2,1,2,2]`, 4 units dropped at index 3:

blocks.h: Why must `best` update only on strict decreases?
p: Take `[2,1,1,2]` with a drop at index 3: the water flows left over two equal cells at height 1. The correct landing spot is the one closest to where the drop started, index 2, not index 1. Because `best` changes only when the next cell is strictly lower, the second equal cell (index 1) does not replace it, and the walk continues past it only if something even lower exists.

blocks.h: Why stop walking when a higher cell appears?
p: Water can't climb a higher cell, so everything beyond it is unreachable. The `while` condition `<=` ends the walk there.

bullets: Space: O(1) (the array is modified in place).

755.takeaway: Pour water: simulate each drop, scanning left then right for the nearest lowest reachable cell, using strict decreases to prefer the closest spot.
